sentences.text: The holotype specimen of Baryonyx — the specimen the species is based on — was estimated to be between 7.5 and 10 meters long and weigh between 1.2 and 2 metric tons.
This large predator stood approximately 2.5 meters tall at the hip.
Its skull was estimated to be 91 to 95 centimeters long based on comparisons with the larger genus Suchomimus, where the total skull length is estimated at 950 millimeters.
The first finger of the holotype specimen bore a large claw measuring about 31 centimeters along its curve.
In 1997, Charig and Milner found the first evidence of fish-eating in a theropod dinosaur in the stomach of a Baryonyx specimen, which contained fish scales, teeth, and iguanodontian bones.
An apparent gizzard stone was found with the Baryonyx holotype specimen.
In 2020, researchers stated that Baryonyx is the oldest confirmed spinosaurid, though older fossils have been tentatively assigned to the group.
The first skeleton of Baryonyx was discovered in 1983 at the Smokejack Clay Pit in Surrey, England, by amateur fossil collector William J. Walker.
Richard Owen named the species Suchosaurus cultridens in 1841 based on teeth found by Gideon A. Mantell in Tilgate Forest.
In 1999, fossils from the Salas de los Infantes deposit in Spain were attributed to an immature Baryonyx.

Baryonyx was the first theropod dinosaur proven to be piscivorous, based on fish scales found in the stomach region of the holotype, which included the fish Scheenstia mantelli and bones of a young Iguanodon.

Baryonyx had crocodile-like adaptations including long narrow jaws with a terminal rosette and a snout with a downturned tip and notch, suggesting it caught and swallowed prey like a gharial, a similarity supported by a 2007 study on snout biomechanics.

A 2016 study found that adult spinosaurs could move the halves of their lower jaw sideways to widen the throat opening, allowing them to swallow large prey, a trait also noted in a 2016 study comparing spinosaurid jaws to those of the pike fish.

Researchers speculated that Baryonyx's elongated skull, long neck, and strong humerus indicated it was a facultative quadruped, a trait unique among theropods, though paleontologists Hone and Holtz suggested that spinosaurid forelimbs were not optimal for trapping prey but appeared similar to those of digging animals.
Portuguese Baryonyx fossils found with isolated iguanodontian teeth support the idea that spinosaurs were opportunistic feeders.
Baryonyx likely caught fish and scavenged on mud plains, possibly becoming trapped in mud before dying.
Baryonyx is now classified as a member of the family Spinosauridae, whereas researchers originally classified it in its own family, Baryonychidae, because it was considered unique among theropods.
In 2021, Barker and colleagues supported a European origin for spinosaurids that expanded to Asia and Gondwana in the early Early Cretaceous.

Baryonyx lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 130 to 125 million years ago, in the Weald Clay Formation, which dates from the Hauterivian to Barremian ages, in what is now Europe.
It lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 130 to 125 million years ago in the Aptian stage, in what is now Europe.
The environment where the holotype died was likely suitable for a fish-eating animal.

It is debated whether Suchosaurus cultridens is a senior synonym of Baryonyx or if Suchomimus tenerensis belongs in the same genus. Thomas R. Holtz and colleagues raised the possibility in 2004 that a maxilla fragment from Spain belonged to Suchomimus rather than Baryonyx. In 2003, Milner concurred that spinosaurid material from Niger was indistinguishable from Baryonyx.
